1.title: Quick-Reference Recap
1.text: Welcome to Module fourteen, the quick-reference recap. This module has no new content and no practice questions. It gathers the comparisons, the glossary and a decision aid from modules one to thirteen onto single pages, so you can scan them in the last days before the exam.

1.title: How to Use This Recap
1.text: Nothing here is new. Every page repeats what the earlier modules taught, in a form you can scan. Cover and recall: hide the right-hand side of a table, answer from memory, then check. Follow the module tags to go back to the detail. Mind the tags: pages marked Dates or Verify live hold facts that change, so confirm them before the exam. Numbers and dates are as of the dated line on each tagged page. Use the recap to find gaps, not to replace the modules.

1.title: The Exam Map: Four Domains, Thirteen Competencies
1.text: The exam map. Domain one, foundations, carries sixteen to twenty questions: harms and principles, roles and training, and policies. Domain two, laws, standards and frameworks, carries nineteen to twenty-three: privacy laws, other existing laws, A I-specific laws, and standards and frameworks. Domain three, governing development, carries twenty-one to twenty-five: the use case, design, data, testing, release and monitoring. Domain four, governing deployment and use, also carries twenty-one to twenty-five. The ranges show weight, not a promise. Exam tip: every question counts the same, so spread your revision across all four domains.

1.title: Roles by Law
1.text: Roles by law. A I Act roles follow the system: provider, deployer, importer, distributor and authorized representative. G D P R roles follow the personal data: controller, processor, and joint controllers under G D P R Article twenty-six. One organization can hold several roles. Helios is a deployer of the hiring tool and a provider of the assistant built on a model it uses. Roles can change: putting your name on a high-risk system, or modifying it substantially, makes a deployer a provider, under Article twenty-five. Processors work under a contract with set terms, under Article twenty-eight. Exam tip: identify the role first.

1.title: EU AI Act Risk Tiers and What Each Brings
1.text: The A I Act sorts systems into tiers. Prohibited, under Article five: manipulation, exploiting vulnerabilities, social scoring, crime prediction by profiling, face-scraping, workplace and school emotion inference, and more. High-risk, under Article six: the Annex three areas, such as employment, and safety components under Annex one. Transparency, under Article fifty: people told they interact with A I, and synthetic content marked. Minimal risk: no specific duties. And general-purpose models, under Articles fifty-one, fifty-three and fifty-five, with extra duties for systemic risk. Exam tip: classify by use, then read off the duties for that tier and your role.

1.title: Provider and Deployer Duties Side by Side
1.text: For a high-risk system, the provider builds and proves conformity. It meets the requirements in Articles nine to fifteen, runs a quality management system under Article seventeen, and completes the conformity steps in Articles forty-three, forty-seven, forty-eight and forty-nine. In use, it supplies instructions under Article thirteen, monitors after release under Article seventy-two, and reports serious incidents under Article seventy-three. The deployer, under Article twenty-six, follows the instructions, assigns competent oversight, checks input data, monitors, and keeps logs for at least six months. Where it applies, it adds the fundamental rights impact assessment of Article twenty-seven. Exam tip: the provider proves the product; the deployer governs the use.

1.title: Penalties Compared
1.text: Penalties compared. Under A I Act Article ninety-nine, prohibited practices carry fines up to thirty-five million euros or seven percent of worldwide turnover. Most other obligations: fifteen million or three percent. Incorrect or misleading information: seven and a half million or one percent. The higher amount applies, but for small and medium-sized enterprises and start-ups, the lower applies. Under Article one hundred and one, the Commission may fine general-purpose model providers up to three percent or fifteen million. The G D P R, Article eighty-three, point five, reaches twenty million or four percent. Exam tip: the A I Act's top tier is reserved for prohibited practices.

1.title: Timelines at a Glance
1.text: The timeline. Second of February, twenty twenty-five: the first prohibitions and the A I literacy duty. Second of August, twenty twenty-five: general-purpose model rules, governance and penalties. Second of August, twenty twenty-six: the Act applies generally. Second of December, twenty twenty-six: new prohibitions. Second of December, twenty twenty-seven: Annex three high-risk systems. Second of August, twenty twenty-eight: Annex one high-risk systems. And the ninth of December, twenty twenty-six: the Product Liability Directive applies to products placed on the market from then. As of the twenty-seventh of October, twenty twenty-six, the Digital Omnibus on A I moved some dates, so confirm them.

1.title: Privacy Law and AI Law Compared
1.text: Compare the two laws on four questions. What it protects: the G D P R protects people's personal data and rights; the A I Act regulates A I systems by risk. When it applies: the G D P R applies to any processing of personal data, with or without A I; the A I Act applies to systems placed on the Union market or whose output is used there. The tools differ: lawful basis, principles, rights and the D P I A under Article thirty-five, against tiers, requirements and conformity. And they overlap: a system that processes personal data is under both, and the fundamental rights impact assessment may cross-refer to a D P I A. Exam tip: check both laws.

1.title: NIST, ISO and OECD Compared
1.text: Three instruments, three natures. The N I S T A I R M F one point zero is voluntary: four functions, Govern, Map, Measure and Manage, in nineteen categories and seventy-two subcategories, with profiles and a Playbook. I S O forty-two thousand and one is a management system standard: clauses four to ten, Annex A with thirty-eight controls in nine objectives, and it is certifiable. The O E C D A I Principles are non-binding: five values-based principles and recommendations for policy makers. At Helios they work together. I S O structures the program, N I S T runs risk per system, the E U A I Act is the legal floor, and the O E C D principles are the basis of policy. Exam tip: match each to its nature.

1.title: The Life Cycle and Where Each Control Sits
1.text: Controls follow the life cycle. Plan and design, from module eight: use-case approval, impact assessment, oversight design and metrics. Data and build, module nine: data governance, lineage, testing, fairness metrics and the model card. Release, module ten: the readiness gate, conformity, staged release and rollback. Deploy, modules eleven to thirteen: context, model and option, assessment of the chosen system, contract, training and oversight. And monitor, maintain and retire, modules ten and thirteen: monitoring, drift, periodic checks, incidents and deactivation. Exam tip: find the life-cycle stage first, then pick the control that belongs to it.

1.title: Reporting Clocks at a Glance
1.text: Reporting clocks. Under A I Act Article seventy-three, a provider reports a serious incident not later than fifteen days after awareness, two days for a widespread infringement, and ten days after a death. Under G D P R Article thirty-three, a personal data breach is notified without undue delay and, where feasible, within seventy-two hours. A processor tells the controller without undue delay. A deployer informs the provider and suspends use where there is a risk, under Article twenty-six. Contracts may set shorter notices. Exam tip: one event can start several clocks, and the shortest applicable one governs.

1.title: Glossary 1: Concepts and Risks
1.text: Glossary one: concepts and risks. A I system: a machine-based system that infers how to generate outputs. Generative A I: creates new content. Predictive model: scores, classifies or predicts. General-purpose A I model: a broad model used in many downstream systems. Confabulation: confident but false output. Bias: a systematic skew. Fairness: comparable outcomes for comparable people. Impact ratio: one group's selection rate over another's. Explainability: giving reasons. Transparency: openness about what a system does. Robustness: holding up under noise or attack. Drift: a shift over time. Overfitting: memorizing training data. Data leakage: test data leaking into training. Automation bias: over-trusting the output. Human oversight: a person who can understand, override and stop. Red teaming: trying to make a system fail. Prompt injection: hidden instructions that hijack a model. Model card: a plain record of use and limits. Data lineage: the traceable path of data.

1.title: Glossary 2: Roles, Law and Assessment
1.text: Glossary two: roles, law and assessment. Provider: develops and places a system on the market. Deployer: uses a system under its authority. Importer: brings a non-Union system to the market. Distributor: passes a system along the supply chain. Controller: decides purposes and means. Processor: processes on the controller's behalf. D P I A: data protection impact assessment. F R I A: fundamental rights impact assessment. High-risk system: an Annex one or Annex three system with full duties. Prohibited practice: a banned use under Article five. Conformity assessment: the check before market placement. C E marking: the sign that conformity was shown. Systemic risk: risk from the largest general-purpose models. Serious incident: death, serious harm or major disruption. Instructions for use: the provider's guide for deployers. Technical documentation: the record of design and testing. Substantial modification: a change needing a new assessment. Post-market monitoring: the provider's watch on a system in use.

1.title: Glossary 3: Frameworks and Practice
1.text: Glossary three: frameworks and practice. Govern, Map, Measure, Manage: the four N I S T functions. Profile: a N I S T view of a use case, a time or a sector. Playbook: N I S T's suggested actions. Statement of applicability: the I S O list of chosen controls. O E C D principles: non-binding values for trustworthy A I. Three lines: management, risk oversight and internal audit. Risk appetite: the level of risk the organization accepts. Risk register: risks with owners and controls. Incident register: incidents and near misses. Change control: test, approve, release, monitor. Kill switch: a tested way to stop a system. Fallback: a manual or older process. Localize: limit a system by region or feature. Indemnity: the vendor's promise to defend and pay. Shadow A I: A I used without registration. Pre-mortem: imagine the failure, then work out why. Staged release: a small share first, then wider. Rollback: return to the previous version.

1.title: Which Instrument Applies? A Decision Aid
1.text: A decision aid. Personal data involved? Look at the G D P R, with a D P I A where the risk is high. An A I system on the E U market, or output used in the E U? The A I Act: classify the tier, then the role. Hiring in New York City? Local Law one hundred forty-four: a bias audit and notice. A defective product causing harm? The Product Liability Directive. A certifiable management system? I S O forty-two thousand and one. Voluntary risk guidance? The N I S T A I R M F. Policy values? The O E C D principles. Exam tip: name the situation, the role and the life-cycle stage first; the instrument usually follows.
